At the municipal library in San Pablo, staff noticed that weekend borrowing increased after they extended opening hours. The new schedule helped workers who could not visit on weekdays. However, the librarians did not yet know whether visitors were actually reading more books. Some patrons borrowed several titles but returned them unopened. To understand the difference, the library began offering an optional one-minute reading reflection at the return desk. Participation remained voluntary, and the librarians kept the responses separate from the borrowers' identifying information. After three weekends, reflections were more common among first-time borrowers than among regular patrons. The director cautioned against claiming that the longer hours had improved literacy. She explained that access, borrowing, reading, and comprehension are related but different outcomes. Before changing the schedule permanently, the staff planned to compare several months of data, including school holidays and bad-weather weekends. The library also tracked the days when school examinations reduced visits, since an unusually quiet weekend could reflect students' schedules rather than changing interest in books. The staff treated those notes as context for later comparisons.

Which conclusion is best supported by the library's findings?

All weekend borrowers finished every book they took home.
Extended hours improved access for some patrons, but better reading comprehension has not been established.
The library must eliminate weekday opening hours to improve access.
